title: Mooncakes sell for only two months a year, yet they've become a 28.2 billion yuan business
dek: Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
why: Worth listening for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand the holiday consumption business, but information density is low — much of the runtime is spent on explaining regional styles and flavors, with the business mechanics concentrated in the middle and later sections.
who: Food industry founders, brands doing corporate custom gifts, and investors wanting to understand the logic of holiday consumption businesses.
skip: 0:12-2:03 Personal taste preferences and Taiwan date paste pastry — unrelated to business analysis.

points.h: Zongzi can sell year-round, mooncakes cannot
points.body: Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all year round — Wufangzhai even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday scenarios. Mooncakes' problem isn't that the craft can't achieve long shelf life, it's that they're defined as "traditional festival pastries mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival" — the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from its festival through shelf life and channels, mooncakes cannot.

points.h: The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
points.body: Lotus paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use the five kernels: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of these lines is to push up ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, red and green shreds, and inferior nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the order of ingredients on the label tells you how much of what is actually in there.

points.h: Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
points.body: Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess but because of structure. Outside is pastry, the middle is a custard layer, and the innermost is the lava layer — the custard layer acts as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point must be engineered: solid during transport, then a few seconds in the microwave turns it into flowing liquid. If heated too long, the lava gets absorbed by the pastry and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

points.h: Five preconditions for "everything can be a mooncake"
points.body: Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot and sour soup mooncakes can't be made because there's too much water to contain. Second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also favored by microorganisms, so processing temperatures and sterilization processes must be repeatedly tested. Third is particle size — too large and the pastry can't contain it, too fine and you can't taste it. Fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply disappear once baked. Fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are ones confirmed by generation after generation.

points.h: Choosing an OEM isn't a matter of bigger is better
points.body: When big brands make branded mooncakes through OEM, there's a common misconception: you must pick the best OEM in the country. But the top OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days without safety incidents. Also, the nine major regional styles correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they don't have that capability or production line.

points.h: Flexible production lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
points.body: Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — wrapping and forming machines can do their part, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes too. If a company has only 50 employees, they can use the factory's existing mooncakes directly and only need to design the box. This small-batch quick-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can do corporate custom business.

points.h: The 28.2 billion yuan scale is propped up by gifting
points.body: In 2025 China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons, with sales of 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion pieces — across a population of 1.4 billion, an average of three to four per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales are about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. Mooncakes selling for only two months a year yet reaching 28.2 billion is fundamentally about the gifting attribute — brands prepare large amounts of PR gifts at the two nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

points.h: 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
points.body: In 2022 the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement placing boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit under key supervision. So the highest price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it's impossible to exceed 500. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor inside, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

points.h: Mini package is becoming a trend
points.body: In the food industry these past two years there's a clear trend called mini package — packaging made smaller. On one hand it can be finished in one sitting after opening; on the other, consumers just want a quick treat and don't want to eat that much, and small packaging also lets you buy many flavors at once. Mooncakes are moving in this direction too, because it's hard for one person to finish a whole mooncake — usually it's cut into several pieces to share. Made smaller, one person can at least finish one, and it reduces waste.

points.h: New flavors die before reaching consumers
points.body: Brands launch five new flavors each year to see which gets eliminated, but a flavor having no repeat purchase doesn't necessarily mean consumers don't like it — it may simply never have reached consumers. Because most mooncakes are gifts, constantly being regifted and circulated, the recipient may pass it on without ever eating it. So next year they won't want to buy that flavor either, because they didn't get to taste it this year. Brands with physical stores have the advantage of doing tastings, letting consumers try before deciding.

A food industry trend of making packaging smaller so it can be finished in one sitting, and so multiple flavors can be bought at once.

quotes.text: I think we have pastries and cakes 365 days a year — it's just that what we normally eat isn't called a mooncake.
It's not that everything can be forced into a mooncake. A long-term stable flavor is definitely something confirmed as OK by generation after generation.
This big OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours.
If you take it out of the Mid-Autumn time slot, or take away the round shape, it's really just a pastry.
A flavor with no repeat purchase doesn't necessarily mean consumers don't like it — it may be that it never reached consumers at all.
Brands and channels alike no longer want to consider making a long-term classic that gets passed down forever. What everyone wants is rapid iteration.
